summary: This document introduces a collection of common data types for the YANG data modeling language. It obsoletes RFC 6021 and has itself been replaced by RFC 9911.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language used to describe the configuration and state of network devices. This RFC provides the standard vocabulary of data types for it: counters that only go up, gauges that can go up and down, addresses, prefixes, port numbers, timestamps and domain names, each with a fixed set of allowed values.

subtitle: The shared data types that YANG modules use for counters, addresses, port numbers, names and times.

tldr.problem: Every YANG module needs types for the same ordinary things, and if each module defines its own, the same value means different things in different models.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two YANG modules of derived types. The ietf-yang-types module holds generally useful types such as counters, gauges, identifiers and timestamps, and the ietf-inet-types module holds Internet-specific ones such as IP addresses, prefixes, port numbers, autonomous system numbers and domain names.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6991 was a Proposed Standard and it obsoleted RFC 6021. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 9911.

sections.title: Why Common YANG Types
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF). The language supports a small set of built-in data types and provides mechanisms to derive other types from the built-in types.

This document introduces a collection of common data types derived from the built-in YANG data types. The derived types are designed to be applicable for modeling all areas of management information, and the definitions are organized in several YANG modules: the ietf-yang-types module contains generally useful data types, and the ietf-inet-types module contains definitions that are relevant for the Internet protocol suite. The document adds new type definitions to the YANG modules and obsoletes RFC 6021; the revision statements of the modules in sections 3 and 4 give the details.

Every type in these modules is a derived type, which means it is a built-in YANG type narrowed by a restriction: a range, a length, a pattern that the text must match, or a list of allowed values. A module that uses one of these types therefore inherits its meaning without having to state it again.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every model inventing its own idea of a counter or an IP address, this RFC fixes the standard ones. A model that uses the standard port-number type then means the same thing as any other model that does.

sections.title: The Two Modules and Their Types
sections.content:
The RFC gives a short overview of the types and their equivalent SMIv2 data types, and a YANG data type is equivalent to an SMIv2 data type if the two have the same set of values and the semantics of the values are equivalent. Where no SMIv2 counterpart exists, the table shows a dash.

The ietf-yang-types module defines counter32, zero-based-counter32, counter64, zero-based-counter64, gauge32, gauge64, object-identifier, object-identifier-128, yang-identifier, date-and-time, timeticks, timestamp, phys-address, mac-address, xpath1.0, hex-string, uuid and dotted-quad. The SMIv2 equivalents for the counters and gauges come from SNMPv2-SMI, with the zero-based and 64-bit variants from RMON2-MIB and HCNUM-TC.

The ietf-inet-types module defines ip-version, dscp, ipv6-flow-label, port-number, as-number, ip-address, ipv4-address, ipv6-address, the matching no-zone variants, ip-prefix, ipv4-prefix, ipv6-prefix, domain-name, host and uri. Their SMIv2 equivalents, where they exist, come from INET-ADDRESS-MIB, DIFFSERV-DSCP-TC, IPV6-FLOW-LABEL-MIB and URI-TC-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The types are split in two: general ones such as counters and timestamps, and Internet ones such as addresses and port numbers. The RFC also lists the SNMP type that each one matches, so that a value means the same thing in both worlds.

sections.title: Counters, Gauges, Identifiers and Time
sections.content:
The counter32 type represents a non-negative integer that monotonically increases until it reaches a maximum value of 2^32-1, 4294967295 decimal, when it wraps around and starts increasing again from zero. Counters have no defined initial value, so a single value of a counter has in general no information content, and discontinuities in the monotonically increasing value normally occur at re-initialization of the management system. The counter32 type should not be used for configuration schema nodes, and a default statement SHOULD NOT be used with it.

The zero-based-counter32 type is a counter32 with the defined initial value of zero: a schema node of this type is set to zero on creation and then increases until it wraps. The counter64 and zero-based-counter64 types are the 64-bit versions, and the gauge32 and gauge64 types represent a non-negative integer that may increase or decrease but shall never exceed a maximum value nor fall below a minimum value. A gauge holds its maximum value whenever the information being modelled is greater than or equal to that maximum, and its minimum value whenever the information is smaller than or equal to the minimum.

The object-identifier type represents administratively assigned names in a registration-hierarchical-name tree, as a sequence of numerical non-negative sub-identifier values separated by single dots, each of which must not exceed 2^32-1. The ASN.1 standard restricts the first sub-identifier to 0, 1 or 2, restricts the second to 0 to 39 when the first is 0 or 1, and requires at least two sub-identifiers. This type is a superset of the SMIv2 OBJECT IDENTIFIER type, since it is not restricted to 128 sub-identifiers, so the object-identifier-128 type should be used to represent the SMIv2 type.

The date-and-time type is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for dates and times using the Gregorian calendar, defined by the date-time production in section 5.6 of RFC 3339. The canonical format for a value with a known time zone uses a numeric offset calculated from the device's configured offset to UTC, and the canonical format for a value with an unknown time zone uses the offset -00:00. The timestamp type is the value of the sysUpTime object at which a specific occurrence happened, and timeticks is a period measured in hundredths of a second.
sections.plainLanguage: A counter only goes up and wraps around at its maximum. A gauge can go up and down but stays between its limits. Object identifiers are dotted numbers, dates are written in the RFC 3339 form, and timestamps count hundredths of a second since the device started.

sections.title: Internet-Specific Types
sections.content:
The port-number type represents a 16-bit port number of an Internet transport-layer protocol such as UDP, TCP, DCCP or SCTP, with a range of 0 to 65535. Port numbers are assigned by IANA, and the value zero is reserved, so in situations where zero does not make sense it can be excluded by subtyping the port-number type.

The as-number type represents autonomous system numbers, which identify an Autonomous System: a set of routers under a single technical administration, using an interior gateway protocol and common metrics to route packets within the AS, and using an exterior gateway protocol to route packets to other ASes. Autonomous system numbers were originally limited to 16 bits, but BGP extensions have enlarged the space to 32 bits, so this type uses an uint32 base type with no range restriction.

The ip-address type represents an IP address and is IP version neutral, with the format of the textual representation implying the IP version; it supports scoped addresses by allowing zone identifiers in the address format. The ipv4-address type represents an IPv4 address in dotted-quad notation, and the ipv6-address type represents an IPv6 address in full, mixed, shortened and shortened-mixed notation. A zone index is used to disambiguate identical address values, typically the interface index number or the name of an interface for link-local addresses, and if it is not present the default zone of the device is used. The matching no-zone types exist for situations where the zone is known from the context.

The ip-prefix types represent an address prefix, with the prefix length given by the number after the slash, at most 32 for IPv4 and at most 128 for IPv6, and the canonical form has all bits outside the prefix set to zero. The dscp type represents a Differentiated Services Code Point with a range of 0 to 63, and the ipv6-flow-label type represents the flow label in an IPv6 packet header, with a range of 0 to 1048575.

The domain-name type represents a DNS domain name, with a length of 1 to 253 characters, and the name SHOULD be fully qualified whenever possible. Internet domain names are only loosely specified, so the pattern is intended to allow for current practice and some possible future expansion. Because the encoding of names in the DNS protocol is limited to 255 characters, and consists of labels prefixed by a length byte with a trailing NULL byte, only 253 characters can appear in the textual dotted notation. Domain-name values use US-ASCII encoding, their canonical format uses lowercase US-ASCII characters, and internationalized domain names must be A-labels. The host type represents either an IP address or a DNS domain name, and the uri type represents a Uniform Resource Identifier, which must be in US-ASCII and normalized as described in RFC 3986.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet types fix the allowed values: a port number is 16 bits, an autonomous system number is 32 bits, a DSCP value is 0 to 63, and a domain name is at most 253 characters written in lowercase. The address types accept a zone index after a percent sign so that the same address can be told apart on different links.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the document defines common data types using the YANG data modeling language, and that the definitions themselves have no security impact on the Internet, but the usage of these definitions in concrete YANG modules might have. The security considerations spelled out in the YANG specification apply for this document as well.

The RFC also registers two URIs in the IETF XML registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-types for the ietf-yang-types module and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-inet-types for the ietf-inet-types module.
sections.plainLanguage: The types themselves are harmless. What matters is how a module uses them, so the security rules of the YANG specification apply to them in the same way.

viz.caption: THE INTERNET-SPECIFIC TYPES AT A GLANCE

items.title: port-number
items.text: A 16-bit transport port, from 0 to 65535, assigned by IANA.

items.title: ip-address
items.text: An IPv4 or IPv6 address, with an optional zone index.

items.title: ip-prefix
items.text: An address and a prefix length, at most 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6.

items.title: domain-name
items.text: A DNS name of up to 253 characters, canonically in lowercase.

items.title: dscp
items.text: A Differentiated Services Code Point, from 0 to 63.

viz.caption: A TYPEDEF FROM THE ietf-yang-types MODULE

data.title: counter32
data.code:
typedef counter32 {
  type uint32;

  description
   "The counter32 type represents a non-negative integer
    that monotonically increases until it reaches a
    maximum value of 2^32-1 (4294967295 decimal), when it
    wraps around and starts increasing again from zero.

    Counters have no defined 'initial' value, and thus, a
    single value of a counter has (in general) no information
    content."
